The pencil on the ruler in the opener is the picture the lesson keeps returning to: a slice is stop minus start.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): python-strings-and-slices-hook (the pencil sum, covered by the opener) and -index-check (covered by the first screen and the slice question).

lesson.title: Take exactly the text you need

lead.text: Take the word CRAYON. Python sees six characters in a row, and each one has a number called its index, which says how far along the row it sits. The first character is zero steps along, so C has index 0. R is one step along, so it has index 1. The row ends with N at index 5. Counting from zero feels odd at first, but a ruler does the same, because its first mark is 0.

You ask for a character by writing the word and then its index in square brackets. With word = 'CRAYON', word[2] is 'A'. The function len(word) gives the number of characters, which is 6, so the last index is always one less than the length. You can also count back from the end. A negative index starts at the far side, so word[-1] is the last character, N, and word[-2] is the one before it.

One character at a time is slow when you want a whole piece of a word. For that you give two numbers with a colon between them, as in word[1:4], and the result is called a slice. Picture a ruler laid along the word with its marks falling between the characters: mark 0 sits before the first character, and each further mark sits after the next one. A slice runs from its start mark to its stop mark.

So word[1:4] takes everything between marks 1 and 4, which is the characters at index 1, 2 and 3. The start is included and the stop is left out, and that is why a slice is as long as the stop minus the start. Step through the picture, where label[1:4] takes 'LAN' out of 'PLANET'.

afterFigure.text: Check it against the ruler. The piece between marks 1 and 4 is 4 − 1 = 3 characters long, just as the pencil in the opening was 5 − 2 = 3 cm. The second case in the picture counts from the end. The slice label[-2:] starts two marks from the end and, because the stop is empty, carries on to the end of the word, which gives 'ET'.

lead.text: A slice takes the characters from its start up to, but leaving out, its stop. Apply that to the word below.

A slice does not need both numbers. If the start is missing, the slice begins at the front of the word, so word[:3] gives the first three characters. A missing stop sends it to the end, so word[3:] gives everything from index 3 onwards. Missing both, word[:] is the whole word.

Negative numbers work in a slice as they do for a single character, by counting back from the end. That makes it easy to take the last few characters of a word without knowing how long it is. The slice word[-5:] starts five back from the end and runs to the end, so it always gives the last five characters, whatever the word. It is the tool for pulling a file extension or a country code off the end of some text.

steps.headline: Take the last four characters of 'HARVEST'.

lead.text: The same two ideas, a negative start and an empty stop, take a piece off the end.

workedSteps.text: A negative start counts back from the end. Four back from the end is -4.
Leaving the stop empty means: carry on to the end of the string.
Positions start at 0. The slice starts at position 1 and stops before position 5.
Count the positions from 1 up to, but not including, 5. How many is that?

lead.text: Slicing takes text apart. Often the job is to tidy it, because data arrives with stray spaces and mixed capitals. Python gives every string a set of built-in actions called methods. You call a method by putting a dot after the string, then the method's name with brackets after it. The method name.strip() removes spaces from both ends of name, and name.upper() turns its letters into capitals.

A method cannot edit the string it was called on, because a string cannot be changed once it exists. It builds a new string and hands it back, and the original stays exactly as it was. To keep the tidy version, store it under a name, as in clean = name.strip().upper().

afterFigure.text: In the picture, the first case stores the cleaned text under clean, and name still holds the padded original. The second case runs the same methods but stores nothing, so the tidy text is made and thrown away at once. Methods can be chained like this: strip runs first, and upper runs on whatever strip handed back.

lead.text: A string method builds a new string. Think about what becomes of that new string when the line does not store it anywhere.

Some characters are invisible, and a line break is one of them. Inside a quoted string you write a line break as a backslash followed by the letter n. Python turns those two keystrokes into a single newline character. This kind of shorthand is called an escape. A string with an escape between two letters holds three characters and prints on two lines.

The code you see does not always match the length Python reports. The function len counts the characters in the finished string, and an escape adds one, no matter how many keystrokes it took. Spaces and tabs add to it too, so stray spaces at the ends of data are worth removing.
Count the characters in the finished string, which may not match the keystrokes you typed.

steps.headline: Past the end of the word

lead.text: Slices are forgiving at the edges. If the stop is larger than the word, the slice quietly ends at the last character, so 'ABCDEF'[3:20] is 'DEF'. If the start lies beyond the end, nothing sits between the marks and the result is an empty string, one with no characters at all. A slice never raises an error for numbers that are too large.

A single index is different. Asking for 'ABCDEF'[20] names a character that does not exist, and Python stops the program with an IndexError. That is why slices are the safer choice for short or messy input: they return whatever is there, even if that is nothing. A field shorter than you expected will not break the program, though it may leave you with an empty piece, so check the length when the piece matters.
Picture the ruler laid along the word, and ask where the two marks of the slice fall.

blocks.text: Hold a ruler against a pencil so that the tip lines up with the 2 cm mark and the other end with the 5 cm mark. The pencil is 3 cm long, and you find that by taking one mark away from the other. The marks do the counting, and the first of them is 0.

Text in a program can be measured the same way. A product code, a surname or a date written out in full is a row of characters, and data arrives full of them, usually with something extra attached: spaces at the ends, capitals where you wanted lower case, a year stuck to the front of an order number. Pulling out exactly the piece you need is a job you will do again and again.

This lesson lays a ruler along a word. You learn to name each character by its position and to cut out a piece by giving two marks, and then to clean text up. The last stop is the end of the ruler, where Python is more forgiving than you might expect.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count positions from zero, cut text with [start:stop], and know which string methods change the original.

recap.keyIdea: Positions count from zero. A slice includes its start and excludes its stop, and a string method hands back a new string rather than changing the old one.

blocks.text: Back at the ruler, a slice measures stop minus start. You counted 3 characters in 'ORCHARD'[2:5] and 4 in 'LANTERN'[1:5], saw that a method's tidy result is lost unless you store it, and found that a slice past the end of 'AB' leaves nothing.

recap.nextHook: Text cannot be changed in place, but a list can, and that has a surprising result when two names lead to one list. The next lesson begins with two keys cut for the same locker.

questions.prompt: After name = '  hill  ', what does name.strip() do if its result is ignored?
hints: Strings cannot be changed in place.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: strip returns a new string. Without assignment, name still refers to the original padded text.

questions.onCorrect: It leaves name unchanged. strip returns a new string, and nothing stored it.

misconceptions.feedback: That would change the string in place. Strings cannot be changed; strip returns a new one.
Nothing is deleted. name still refers to the original text.

questions.prompt: A Python string is written as the letter a, then backslash-n, then the letter b. What is its len?
hints: A newline escape represents one character.
The escape stands for a line break inside the string.
Count a, the newline and b as individual characters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There is one a, one newline and one b: three characters.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Backslash-n is a single newline character, so a, newline and b make three.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the backslash and the n separately. Together they stand for one newline character.

hints: Where does the slice start, and how long is the string?
Position 5 is past the end of a two-character string.
A slice keeps only what lies inside its bounds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The slice starts beyond the available characters, so it is an empty string with 0 characters.

questions.onCorrect: 0. The slice starts beyond the end, so nothing lies inside it. It returns an empty string.

misconceptions.feedback: That returns the whole string. The slice starts after its last character.
That is the gap between the bounds. A slice only keeps characters that exist.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Removing the leading and trailing spaces leaves DATA, which has four characters.

questions.onCorrect: 4. strip returns DATA, with no spaces at either end.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the original string. The question is about the stripped result.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: name is unchanged: space, b, a, y, space is five characters.

questions.onCorrect: 5. The stripped string was thrown away, so name still holds the spaces: one, b, a, y, one.

hints: Where does the pencil start, and where does it end?
Length is the distance between the two marks.
Take the start mark away from the end mark.
questions.prompt: How long is the pencil, in centimetres?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pencil spans from 2 to 5, so 5 − 2 = 3 cm.

questions.onCorrect: 3 cm. The length is the end mark minus the start mark. Slices work the same way: stop minus start.

misconceptions.feedback: That is where the pencil ends on the ruler. Its length is the distance from the tip.
That adds the marks. The length is the gap between them.
